profile.reading:
Iron Mountain Incorporated (NYSE: IRM) is a publicly traded REIT headquartered in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, whose core business is physical and digital records management; its data center division was built substantially through a January 2018 acquisition of IO Data Centers. Per the operator's own site, Iron Mountain's global data center portfolio spans more than 30 locations across three continents totaling roughly 1.4 GW of capacity.

This facility, AZP-1, is part of Iron Mountain's roughly 39-acre Phoenix campus at 615 North 48th Street, Phoenix, Arizona, alongside AZP-2 and a third building, AZP-3, which the operator's own site names but which is not separately tracked as a row in this registry. The Phoenix campus is linked by a 100 Gbps dark-fiber ring to Iron Mountain's separate, roughly 4.5-acre Scottsdale campus (AZS-1). Per the operator, AZP-1 itself carries 41 MW of IT capacity, and the combined Phoenix-plus-Scottsdale footprint totals more than 130 MW across 50-plus acres and 1.4 million-plus square feet.

Iron Mountain's 2018 acquisition of IO Data Centers added four colocation facilities in New Jersey, Ohio, and two in Arizona, per Wikipedia's account of the deal, and IO Data Centers' well-known flagship Phoenix build was commonly reported in the industry as sited near North 48th Street close to Sky Harbor airport, consistent with this address, though this registry has not located a primary source this session that confirms AZP-1 specifically as one of the two acquired Arizona sites rather than a later Iron Mountain build. No year-opened figure, standalone square footage for this building alone, or independently verified Uptime Institute tier certificate was located in sourcing to date.

Iron Mountain trades on the New York Stock Exchange under ticker IRM and files with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission under CIK 0001020569, structured as a real estate investment trust. Records management remains the company's larger, founding business line by facility count; the data center segment is reported separately in Iron Mountain's public filings as a smaller but faster-growing division. Metro Phoenix has grown into one of the largest US data center markets outside the traditional Northern Virginia and Dallas hubs, drawing operators in part on lower land costs and a large regional power grid footprint.
